hypothesis: If the human curve of growth in body length has its point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life, then the velocity of body-length growth (d length / d gestational age) must still be increasing through the end of the first trimester and must already be decreasing through the third trimester, so that the velocity maximum lies between the end of the first trimester and the start of the third (about 14 to 24 completed weeks of gestation, i.e. months 4-6, centred on month 5).
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. Using the 50th-centile curves of international (INTERGROWTH-21st) standards for fetal crown-rump length (9+0 to 14+0 weeks) and for newborn crown-heel length by gestational age at birth (24 to 42 weeks), compute growth velocity in mm/week by finite differences of the median curve. The claim is supported if (a) median CRL velocity averaged over weeks 13-14 exceeds that averaged over weeks 9-10 (length growth still accelerating at 14 weeks), and (b) median crown-heel-length velocity averaged over weeks 24-28 exceeds that averaged over weeks 36-40 and the 24-40 velocity series has a negative linear trend (growth already decelerating from 24 weeks). (a) and (b) together bracket the velocity maximum within 14-24 weeks, which contains 'about the fifth month'. As a secondary check, the gestational age of peak velocity of INTERGROWTH-21st fetal femur length (14-40 weeks) is reported; a femur peak within 14-24 weeks or at the 14-week boundary is consistent with the claim.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted if median CRL velocity is already lower at weeks 13-14 than at weeks 9-10 (velocity maximum before month 4, i.e. before 14 weeks), or if median crown-heel-length velocity at weeks 36-40 is not lower than at weeks 24-28 (velocity maximum after month 6), or if neither measure shows a change of sign in acceleration anywhere in 9-42 weeks (no inflection). A femur-length velocity peak later than 24 weeks also counts against the claim. Any other combination is 'mixed'.
interpretation: Thompson plots 'length' of the human foetus (crown-heel body length from His and other nineteenth-century sources) against age in months and locates an inflection about month five. No modern public standard measures crown-heel length continuously across gestation: ultrasound gives crown-rump length to 14 weeks and skeletal lengths afterwards, and body length is measured directly only at birth. The test therefore brackets the velocity peak from two body-length measures of the same consortium's population: crown-rump length (first trimester) and crown-heel length of newborns by gestational age at birth (24-42 weeks). Gestational ages are menstrual weeks; Thompson's 'fifth month' is taken as roughly 17-22 menstrual weeks, so months 4-6 (14-24 weeks) is the window consistent with 'about the fifth month'. Velocities of the median curve are used because the published standards are smoothed centile tables, not individual-level data. The rOpenSci gigs package redistributes the INTERGROWTH-21st published tables and equations as machine-readable files; those files are used, with the primary publications cited. No data values were inspected before this pre-registration.
